text: The normal distribution, the famous bell curve, is the most important continuous distribution in statistics. It's symmetric, peaked in the middle, and completely described by two numbers — the mean, its center, and the standard deviation, its spread. Confidence intervals and t-tests later in this course lean on it heavily, but it's also over-applied, so this lesson covers both its power and its limits.

A continuous variable can take any value in a range, so the probability of hitting one exact value is zero — instead we talk about the probability of falling within an interval, the area under the curve. The curve's height is the probability density function; the running total of area is the cumulative distribution function.

Suppose delivery times are roughly normal with a mean of 40 minutes and a standard deviation of 5. scipy's norm uses loc for the mean and scale for the standard deviation, not the variance. About 84 percent of deliveries take 45 minutes or less. About 68 percent fall between 35 and 45 minutes — one standard deviation either side of the mean. Only about 2.3 percent take longer than 50 minutes.

ppf, the inverse of the CDF, answers percentile questions — 95 percent of deliveries finish within about 48.2 minutes. For any normal distribution, roughly 68 percent of values fall within 1 standard deviation of the mean, 95 percent within 2, and 99.7 percent within 3 — confirmed directly on the standard normal. A value more than 3 standard deviations out is genuinely rare, which is why analysts treat such points as candidate outliers.

A z-score restates a value as how many standard deviations from the mean, using x minus mean, divided by standard deviation. A 52-minute delivery is 2.4 standard deviations above average, and only about 0.8 percent of deliveries are that slow. Because z-scores strip away units, you can compare a delivery time and an order value on the same scale. A cutoff you'll meet soon, ppf of 0.975, is about 1.96 — where 95 percent intervals come from.

Real data is never perfectly normal, so check it. Drawing 10,000 samples from a true normal distribution and checking the 68 percent rule gives 0.6792, close to the theoretical 0.6827. For real data, use a histogram or Q-Q plot first, and treat skewness as a warning sign — a normal sample has skewness near 0, here 0.007, while a right-skewed exponential sample gave 1.866.

A formal test like scipy's shapiro returns a p-value, but be careful — with huge samples it flags trivial departures, and with tiny samples it misses real ones. Plots plus judgment beat a single test. Don't assume normality just because a method is convenient — incomes, order values, and session lengths are usually right-skewed.

The good news, coming in Lesson 16: averages of many observations behave normally even when the raw data does not. To recap: the normal distribution is set by its mean and standard deviation. Use cdf for areas below a value, sf for above, and ppf for percentiles. The 68-95-99.7 rule gives quick intuition, z-scores put values on a common scale, and you should always check normality with plots rather than assuming it.
